newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain 1997 budget draft to test peseta tranquility.
newsitem.headline: Spain 1997 budget draft to test peseta tranquility.

text.p: Spain's upcoming 1997 budget must be strict and credible or investors may shatter the peseta's recent calm and send it sliding, analysts say.
The new conservative government has pledged to deliver by the end of September an austere budget that will enable Spain to participate in the launch of a common European currency.

Up to now the peseta has been content to wait for the budget draft. It has been drifting in a range between 84.25 and 84.70 to the mark in recent weeks but the budget and the Bank of Spain's reaction to it could unsettle the currency.
At 0825 GMT, the peseta was trading at 84.28/30

"We will have to see the content of the budget to see whether there is a large possibility of adhering to Maastricht (the treaty on Europe's single currency plans). If the accounts aren't as restrictive as expected, the investors might leave (Spain)," said Merrill Lynch analyst Antonio Villarroya.
Nonetheless, Villarroya said that at least on paper the 1997 budget was likely to augur well for Spain's chances of joining the Euro currency's launch in 1999, or at the latest in 2001.
Like many European Union members, Spain's thorniest problem is narrowing its budget deficit to comply with single currency requirements of a three percent ratio to gross domestic product.
The government has pledged to reduce its deficit to the three percent threshhold next year from a projected 4.4 percent this year.

If the government offers a convincing budgetary performance, the Bank of Spain is seen cutting its key money market interest rate for the sixth time this year, having lowered it to the current 7.25 percent from nine percent at the start of the year.

"In recent weeks the peseta has remained trapped between 84.40 and 84.70, with volatility levels near historic minimums. This impasse could continue until there is a trigger, which could be a Bank of Spain rate cut," a currency dealer said.
For many dealers, this could prompt a long slide. Many see the peseta weakening to 85 to the mark by the end of the year and approaching 87 at the end of 1997.

"In the next weeks the peseta could strengthen to 84.20/25, but then, coinciding with the approval of the budget, a cut in rates and more growth in Germany, the conditions are perfect for the peseta to start ceding ground toward the end of the year to 85.50/86.00 per mark," said Cesar Cantalapiedra, economist at Analistas Financieros Internacionales.
The peseta is also likely to be weighed down by France's troubled path to convergence and resulting franc worries.
"The French franc crisis hasn't finished yet," said Cantalapiedra, adding that the franc's underlying weakness had all the peripheral currencies on the rack.
But Villarroya said he saw the peseta strengthening gently towards 83 per mark.

"The peseta is in a relativly balanced situation from the current account and purchasing power parity perspectives, and the expected decline in the differential between inflation and rates could have a beneficial effect on the currency," he added.
